title: Chicken breast, baked, broiled, or roasted, skin eaten, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean, boneless cut taken from the bird’s chest. When baked, broiled, or roasted, it retains a high protein content and low fat, especially when the skin is removed. It is a staple in weight‑controlled diets, sports nutrition, and cuisines worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A 100 g serving provides about 31 g of high‑quality protein, making it one of the richest protein sources among meats.
If the skin is left on, it adds roughly 15 % fat, but removing it drops total fat to under 3 g per 100 g.
Chicken is the most widely produced poultry globally, accounting for over 50 % of all meat and egg production.
Baking at 180 °C preserves most B‑vitamins, especially niacin (vitamin B3).
Chicken breast appears in dishes from sushi rolls to salads and sandwiches across Asian, European, and American cuisines.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Protein supports muscle growth and repair, immune function, and enzyme synthesis.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skin‑less breast contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g, suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Niacin, vitamin B6, and vitamin B12 aid energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, antioxidant defense, and immunity.

items.title: Supports weight management
items.content: The satiety effect of protein can help reduce overall calorie intake.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Added sodium in processed forms
items.content: Pre‑marinated or ready‑to‑eat chicken breasts often contain extra salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Nutrient loss with overcooking
items.content: Excessive heat can degrade B‑vitamins and create harmful compounds such as acrylamide.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken breast can be served hot, sliced thin for salads, formed into patties, baked with herbs and spices, or added to soups. The skin may be kept for extra flavor, but removing it reduces calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh raw breast should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen breast retains quality for up to 9 months at –18 °C. Cooked breast stored in an airtight container lasts 3‑4 days in the fridge.
